sections.h2: Which offices run property tax in Morris County
sections.html:
Property tax in Morris County is a shared job: a county board on one side and 39 town offices on the other. The Morris County Board of Taxation holds the county's records of taxable real estate, sets tax rates and equalization ratios, supervises the municipal assessors, reviews assessments and rules on appeals. Its mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900.

New Jersey leaves budgets to local government, and the state receives none of the property tax money. A town divides the dollars it must raise by the assessed value of everything taxable inside its borders, and that quotient is the general rate. Your bill equals the rate times your own assessment.

  • Your town's assessor sets the number printed on your notice.
  • The county board hears disputes about that number and publishes each town's rate.
  • The Morris County Clerk files the deed once the house closes.

Homeownership runs high and incomes are strong. About 524,251 people live here by the 2025 estimate, against 509,285 in 2020, spread over 193,245 households of 2.62 people on average. Roughly 91.1 percent of residents stayed in the same house for a year, which suggests that many sellers have owned for a long time.

Owners without a mortgage still carry $1,385 a month, and a large share of that is the tax bill and insurance. The land climbs from the flatter Passaic River valley suburbs in the east to hills in the west, and drainage differs between valley floor and ridge, so ask your town's office whether the lot sits near a mapped flood area before you set a price.

sections.h2: How to contest a Morris County assessment
sections.html:
Your petition has to reach the Morris County Board of Taxation by April 1, or May 1 in a town that just revalued or reassessed. Send form A-1 with the comparable sales sheet.

The board will call your value excessive only if it falls outside a set yardstick. After a revaluation, the yardstick is 100 percent of market value on the previous October 1. In other years, the town's common level range is the yardstick, set at plus or minus 15 percent around its average ratio.

  • Use arm's length sales dated before October 1.
  • Plan to appear in person, because the board runs no virtual hearings.
  • If the board's judgment disappoints you, the Tax Court of New Jersey is the next stop, with a 45 day clock.
  • An assessment over $1,000,000 gives the owner a choice to bypass the county board.
  • Added or omitted assessments use form AA-1, with direct Tax Court access above $750,000.

sections.h2: Relief that ends when you sell
sections.html:
All three of Senior Freeze, ANCHOR and Stay NJ are tied to a principal residence, so selling the house ends them for that address. An owner aged 65 or older may qualify for all three, and a renter qualifies for ANCHOR only. Each program has a yearly application window, so look for the next one on the state's relief page.

The state's home sale guide adds two cautions for movers. Say on the application that you moved after October 1, or the benefit can be lost. Anyone in Senior Freeze who buys another New Jersey home waits two years, instead of three, for a new base year.

Separate local deductions exist for seniors and disabled persons and for veteran owners, along with an exemption for a disabled veteran. Your town's tax office administers those, so ask whether the break on your Morris County house stops at closing.

If you are selling a house that a parent or spouse owned, ask the town's tax office whether a deduction from the former owner is still on the account. The new owner may need to file fresh forms, and the next bill will show the difference. Doing this before you list avoids a surprise after the buyer's lender has already priced the monthly payment from the old figure.

Keep a copy of any approval or denial letter you receive. The title company can ask for it, and it is the quickest way to show that a deduction or credit was dealt with properly before the deed changed hands.

sections.h2: What happens at the closing table
sections.html:
When the deed is recorded, the seller owes the state Realty Transfer Fee and files a GIT/REP form alongside it. A seller who remains a New Jersey resident signs GIT/REP-3, which means no deposit, and reports any gain on the NJ-1040 later. Rates sit on the state's Realty Transfer Fee page.

The Registry Department of the Morris County Clerk handles recording, from 8:00 AM to 4:00 PM, at 973-285-6130. Each land document goes in with a cover sheet and a cover letter giving the submitter's name and address, and the document itself carries a "Record & Return" or "Cancel & Return" note.

Get a payoff for any unpaid quarter from your town's tax office, and ask the closing attorney to prorate this year's bill. Those two figures decide what you net from a Morris County sale.

You can still sell a Morris County house that owes tax. Closing pays off the balance and any interest from the seller's share, which makes an accurate figure essential. The town tax office provides it, since the county neither bills nor collects.

  • Call the town tax office and have the payoff run through the day you close.
  • Pass the number to your closing attorney, who also splits the current year's bill between you and the buyer.
  • Confirm the block and lot number, which the deed package needs and the assessor can supply.
  • Mention a pending appeal to your attorney, since a lower value changes what the buyer sees on the record.

Older houses and estate sales often come to market needing a roof or a cleanout. Those houses draw fewer offers, which leaves the owner weighing an as-is sale against months of repairs. A house priced near the county's $582,500 typical value usually draws interest from buyers who already work nearby. A cash buyer skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but the transfer fee, the deed recording and the tax payoff still happen at the same counters, so plan for them in either case.

faqs.q: Where do I file a Morris County property tax appeal?
faqs.a: File with the Morris County Board of Taxation, using Form A-1 and the comparable sales form. The board's mailing address is P.O. Box 900, Morristown, NJ 07963-0900, and hearings take place in person.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for a Morris County tax appeal?
faqs.a: April 1 is the usual receipt date, and May 1 replaces it after a town revaluation or reassessment. Since the board wants the petition in hand by then, send it well ahead of time.

faqs.q: Does Morris County bill my property tax?
faqs.a: No, your municipality bills and collects it. The county board sets rates and equalization ratios and hears appeals, while your town's tax office issues the bill and supplies payoff figures at a sale.

faqs.q: Can a $1.2 million assessment bypass the county board?
faqs.a: Yes, you may take an assessment above $1,000,000 straight to the Tax Court of New Jersey. The same April 1 or May 1 receipt date governs that filing.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer fee on a Morris County sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays at recording. A graduated percent fee also falls on the seller if the price goes above $1,000,000.
